descriptor.scene: There is no human being in this frame and no second capped mascot figure. THE CAMERA HAS WALKED IN CLOSE to one figure and nothing else has changed: the manager fills the frame from the chest up and his head alone is at least a third of the frame height. He stands square and front-on, calm and attentive, mitten arms relaxed at his sides, his cream newsboy cap level on his head, his dot eyes lowered a little toward what stands in front of him. Held up before him at chest height on a small honey-wood easel, ANGLED AWAY from the camera and TOWARD HIM so we read them by their colour and their light rather than square-on, TWO candidate painted pages side by side. The one at the LEFT is the funny page: bright and bouncy, warm yellows, a tumbling round shape mid-fall. The one at the RIGHT is the gentle page: quiet soft creams and muted greens, slow and tender, a small doorway of warm light standing open in it. His attention has settled on the gentle page at the right, and his plum glow falls warmer on that side of the easel. No lettering and no readable text on either page. Behind him the factory is close, warm and softly out of focus. This is the quietest and most weighted picture in the book: stillness, one figure, one decision.
descriptor._caption: Then comes the moment no rail covers. The funny page would get a laugh. But Theo is scared, and scared wants the gentle page. No machine can make that call. This is why the manager's seat takes a manager.
negatives: the two pages squared up flat to the camera
readable text or lettering on either page
a human being of any kind
a wide view; the head must fill a third of the frame height

If a person in this scene is moving toward something, that destination MUST BE AHEAD OF THEM IN THE FRAME and they must be seen FROM BEHIND or from three-quarters behind, so the viewer is following them into it. A figure whose face is toward the camera is walking AWAY from everything behind them: if the thing they are moving toward is drawn behind them, the picture says the opposite of the scene. Their feet, hips, shoulders and gaze all point the same way, along the direction of travel.
